text: Every discrepancy is cleared up now, which means it's finally time to answer the question a percentage alone never answers: so what?
4.1% sounds small until it's set against the actual eligible base, roughly 38,500 customers who were genuinely at risk of churning. That puts the real count at about 1,580 actual people.

Multiplying by an estimated average annual customer value of around $340 turns that count into roughly $537,000 in annual revenue at risk — not revenue already lost, but a real order-of-magnitude estimate of what continued churn costs if nothing changes.

The number gets stated as what it actually is — roughly 1,580 customers, about $540,000 — not as a precise-looking $537,218.44, which would claim a certainty the underlying average simply doesn't have.

A number without a decision attached just gets filed away. A win-back campaign reaching even 20% of these customers would be worth roughly $107,000 a year — the kind of number that actually justifies spending something real on a campaign.
1,580 customers, $540,000 at risk, and a decision worth making. Next up: discovering that number isn't spread evenly at all.
